verified.title: retryFailedEmails is a self-feeding amplification loop that is now exhausting the platform's entire Resend daily sending quota
verified.evidence:
I re-derived every leg of this independently. CODE (lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:72-104, read in full): the SELECT at :75-82 filters on `status = 'failed'` plus a 24h/5min window and nothing else. There is no attempts column, no retried_at, no counter of any kind — directly contradicting the function's own doc comment at :71 ("fewer than 3 retries"). The loop at :86-101 calls sendTemplatedEmail and never touches the source row. sendTemplatedEmail reaches lib/email/adapters/resend.ts:19-37, which INSERTs a fresh email_logs row with status='queued', then UPDATEs that NEW row to 'sent' (:65-70) or 'failed' (:78-83). The original row is untouched, so it is re-selected on the next tick, and the retry's own failure row joins the candidate set. The loop is unbounded by construction. LIVE DATA (all re-run by me): (1) `select template_key,status,count(*),count(distinct "to") from email_logs group by 1,2` -> group_verification_link = 40,857 failed + 3,677 queued + 609 sent = 45,143 rows, all failed/queued rows to exactly 1 distinct recipient. (Finder measured 44,510 on the same key; it has grown 633 rows since.) (2) `select channel,count(*),min(created_at),max(created_at) from registrant_verifications group by 1` -> email channel: 5 rows ALL-TIME, newest 2026-08-16 19:37:12. The first failed group_verification_link row is 2026-08-16 19:34:40 — the loop was seeded by that single request and has run unattended for 19 days. (3) Producer control: job_queue `email_weekly_summary` last COMPLETED 2026-08-24, one failure 2026-08-31, nothing since. Yet email_logs holds weekly_summary rows created on 2026-08-28/29/30/31, 09-01, 09-02, 09-03 and 09-04 (72-87 failed + 21-29 queued per day). The legitimate weekly producer has not run in 12 days; only the retry sweep can be writing those rows. (4) Growth rate re-measured from `date_trunc('day',created_at)`: 09-01 = 1,006 rows, 09-02 = 1,018, 09-03 = 1,036, 09-04 = 790, 09-05 = 371 in the first 7.85 h (~1,134/day pace). The finder's "~1,030/day" is accurate. (5) Provider outcome, re-measured: `UPDATE email_logs SET status=$3, error_message=$1` = 43,546 calls vs `UPDATE email_logs SET status=$3, provider_message_id=$1, sent_at=NOW()` = 706 calls. (6) NEW EVIDENCE the finder did not have — I read the actual error strings. `select template_key,left(error_message,90),count(*) from email_logs where status='failed' and created_at > now()-interval '7 days' group by 1,2`: "You have reached your daily email sending quota." — 706 group_verification_link, 254 staff_operational_alert, 88 weekly_summary, 28 account_statement. "Greeting never received" — 1,570 group_verification_link, 218 staff_operational_alert, 171 weekly_summary, 23 account_statement. (7) NEW: the loop is no longer only failing. Since the EMAIL_FROM repoint on 2026-09-03, group_verification_link 'sent' rows are 200 (09-03), 194 (09-04), 163 (09-05 by 07:50) to one real recipient. (8) Queue impact confirmed directly in Sentry KITABUYETU-1 ("[jobs] queue STARVATION — job types not getting a turn", 600 events, last seen 08:00 UTC today). Its byType payload names email_retry_failed FIRST: pending 4,686, oldestMins 23,430 (16.3 days) — the largest backlog of any job type, ahead of email_campaign_drain (3,732) and mpesa_reconcile (2,899). (9) Rendering claim corrected but upheld. lib/services/email.service.ts:22-35 does produce `

{JSON.stringify(vars)}

` — but only in the .catch branch, which is NOT the path taken here. renderTemplate (lib/email/templates/engine.ts:134-154) finds no DB row (email_templates has 0 rows) and falls back to DEFAULT_TEMPLATES, returning `subject: vars.subject ? String(vars.subject) : 'Kitabu Yetu'`. That is decisive: all 45,143 group_verification_link rows carry the literal subject "Kitabu Yetu", and defaults.ts:29-37 shows the body is `Hi {{name}}`, `verify {{groupName}} ({{groupCode}})`, `href="{{verifyUrl}}"`. With vars={} every retry delivers a verification email with a blank name, a blank group and an EMPTY verify link.
verified.impact:
The finder's severity is right and its impact statement is understated. Three live harms, in order:
(1) QUOTA STARVATION — the loop is consuming the platform's entire Resend daily sending allowance. Real transactional mail is being rejected as collateral: 28 account_statement and 254 staff_operational_alert sends failed in the last 7 days with "You have reached your daily email sending quota", the most recent at 08:00 UTC today. This is not a background inefficiency; it is an active outage of legitimate email caused by junk retries winning the quota race.
(2) LIVE SPAM — since 2026-09-03 the loop is successfully delivering ~200 broken verification emails per day to one real inbox (163 already today), each with a blank group name and a dead link. That is a deliverability/reputation risk on the same Resend domain the platform depends on.
(3) INFRASTRUCTURE — email_logs is 48,221 rows / 22 MB. The email path (retry SELECT + INSERT + both status UPDATEs + template + branding + schedules lookups) is 194,503 statements and 1,384,235 ms = 23.1 min = 6.65% of the database's 346.7 min total exec time, and ~194k of 629,293 BEGINs (31% of all transactions). It holds the #1 job-queue backlog, proven in Sentry KITABUYETU-1.
Correction to the framing: "44,510 emails generated from 5 requests" is right for log rows and outbound API attempts, but only 705 emails have ever actually been delivered platform-wide — the other ~47,500 rows are failures and stranded 'queued' rows.
verified.recommendation: Immediate mitigation, today: stop enqueuing `email_retry_failed` (lib/jobs/index.ts:67-69). The loop has never delivered a correct email in its life, and turning it off instantly returns the Resend daily quota to real member statements and staff alerts. Then fix properly in lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:72-104: (a) add an `attempts` column to email_logs, filter `WHERE attempts < 3`, and UPDATE the source row inside the loop so it cannot be re-selected; (b) mark retry-generated sends (e.g. reference_type='retry') and exclude them from the candidate set so a retry's own failure is never retried; (c) either persist the original `vars` on email_logs and replay them, or delete the retry feature — a retry that cannot reconstruct its variables can only ever send a broken email. Separately one-off DELETE the ~45,000 orphan group_verification_link rows, and treat "You have reached your daily email sending quota" as a hard stop (abort the pass) rather than a per-row failure to be logged 706 times.
verified.note:
Fully reproduced, plus two pieces of evidence the finder missed that both raise the severity: the failures are Resend daily-quota rejections that starve legitimate mail, and since 2026-09-03 the loop is actually delivering. One detail corrected: the delivered body is the DEFAULT_TEMPLATES verification email with every placeholder blanked (subject 'Kitabu Yetu'), not the literal `

{}

` — the finder cited the wrong fallback branch, but its conclusion (the retry cannot produce a useful email) is proven by the template source and by the subject recorded on all 45,143 rows.

verified.title: The retry sweep's SELECT * pulls 210,957 wide rows for the 5 columns it uses, at 5.1% of all database execution time
verified.evidence:
Code re-read: lib/services/scheduler.service.ts:75-83 is `SELECT * FROM email_logs ... LIMIT 50`; the loop body at :86-96 reads exactly five fields — template_key, "to", group_id, reference_id, reference_type. information_schema confirms email_logs has 21 columns.

Re-measured in pg_stat_statements (121-day window): 28,064 calls, 210,957 rows returned, 1,065,783 ms total (17.8 min), mean 37.98 ms. The finder reported 27,894 / 202,457 / 1,028,942 ms — same statement, grown since. Ranking check I added: this is the #4 statement in the whole database by total time at 5.12%, behind pg_net's internal `net._http_response` GC (29.36% + 15.87%) and the job_queue priority scan (17.92%). It is the most expensive statement the application itself owns.

My own EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on live prod: `Index Scan using idx_email_logs_group_id ... Index Cond on created_at ... Rows Removed by Filter: 399 ... rows=780 ... width=343 ... Buffers: shared hit=876 ... Execution Time: 254.9 ms`. I also measured the real row size rather than trusting the planner: `avg(pg_column_size(t.*))` over 2,000 recent failed rows = 245.4 bytes. So ~52 MB shipped over the wire for 5 columns' worth of need — the finder's "roughly 55 MB" is right, though its stated 343 B/row is the planner's estimate, not the measured value.

Index control: I listed all 6 indexes on email_logs. There is no partial index on (created_at) WHERE status='failed'; the planner is falling back to a full scan of idx_email_logs_group_id (group_id, created_at DESC), using created_at as a non-leading Index Cond, which is why 399 of 1,179 scanned rows are discarded. The listing returned 6 rows, so the absence is real.
verified.impact: 17.8 minutes of database execution time (5.1% of the instance's 346.7-min total) and ~52 MB of row data pulled across the network, to read five short columns 210,957 times. Entirely wasted: this is the input side of the amplification loop in finding #1, so the whole cost disappears the moment that loop is bounded. Fixing the projection alone (SELECT five columns instead of *) is still worth doing — it cuts per-row width from ~245 B to ~90 B and is a one-line change — but it treats a symptom.
verified.recommendation: Project the five columns actually consumed. Add `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_email_logs_failed_created ON email_logs (created_at) WHERE status = 'failed'` so the scan stops discarding a third of what it reads. Lower LIMIT 50 to something a Vercel function budget can absorb. Do all of this AFTER (or alongside) bounding the retry loop — on its own it makes a runaway loop cheaper rather than stopping it.
verified.note: Numbers re-measured and all slightly HIGHER than reported, so the magnitude is understated rather than inflated. One causal claim in the original impact does NOT hold and I have dropped it: the finder wrote that sequential provider calls are 'why 897 runs hit the 6-minute stuck-job threshold' and that this 'is exactly what turns a bounded retry into an unbounded loop'. Both are wrong. job_queue shows 4,200 email_retry_failed jobs COMPLETED against 930 failed — 82% of attempts finished — and every failure is dated after 2026-08-20, matching the queue-starvation onset (Sentry oldestMins 23,430) rather than a per-pass timeout. More importantly, the loop is unbounded because there is no retry counter and the source row is never updated; it would be unbounded even if every pass completed in a millisecond. The over-fetch fact stands on its own measurement.

verified.title: SQL join fan-out survives in getPlatformAnalytics — the admin analytics chart plots THE FIONA'S loan book as KES 32.1M instead of KES 1.07M
verified.evidence:
Code re-read at lib/services/admin.service.ts:1318-1330: `groups` is LEFT JOINed to three independent one-to-many tables — group_members (:1324), contributions (:1325), loans (:1326) — and SUM(c.amount) (:1321) and SUM(l.principal_amount) (:1322) are computed over the multiplied row set. COUNT(DISTINCT gm.id) at :1320 is protected; the two SUMs are not. Served by app/api/admin/analytics/route.ts:10 (getPlatformAnalytics), behind cached(..., 120).

I ran the endpoint's exact query against a correlated-subquery control in a single statement on live production and reproduced the finder's numbers exactly:
  THE FIONA'S   — members 5 vs 5 (correct); contributions truth 1,550.00 vs fan-out 31,000.00 (20x); loan_book truth 1,070,000.00 vs fan-out 32,100,000.00 (30x)
  CAPITAL POINT CHAMA — contributions 1,780.00 vs 16,020.00 (9x)
  Joka Ezra     — contributions 310.00 vs 2,170.00 (7x)
Falsification control: the same statement returned exact equality on the other 6 of 9 groups, and member counts matched on all 9 — so the query can and does agree where no fan-out is possible. The three mismatches are real.

Render path confirmed: app/(admin)/admin/analytics/page.tsx:24 reads `data.topGroups` and :159 passes it to <TopGroupsChart>, whose _charts.tsx:54 plots `<Bar dataKey="loan_book" name="Loan Book" />`. The inflated figure is drawn on a chart, not buried in a payload.

DECISIVE ADDITION the finder missed: the repository already documents this exact defect, with this exact number. lib/services/admin-geography.service.ts:18-25 carries the comment "Proven live: Bungoma's loan_book read KES 32,100,000 here vs a real KES 1,070,000 — a 30x inflation — same bug class as admin.service.ts's getGroupById (99x on a single group there)", and :26-35 shows the fix already applied there as per-group correlated subqueries in a CTE.
verified.impact: The superadmin analytics dashboard renders a KES 32.1M loan book for a group whose real book is KES 1.07M — a 31-million-shilling overstatement on the platform's own reporting surface, cached 120s and refreshed indefinitely. `ORDER BY contributions DESC LIMIT 10` at :1328-1329 ranks on the inflated contributions figure, so the "top groups" ordering is corrupt too. Cost is purely correctness (the tables are tiny; the query is not slow). The aggravating factor is that this is a known, diagnosed, already-fixed bug class: the correct pattern sits three files away with a comment naming the identical 32,100,000 / 1,070,000 numbers.
verified.recommendation: Copy the pattern from admin-geography.service.ts:26-35 verbatim — a per-group CTE of correlated subqueries — or the LATERAL form PR #105 used elsewhere. Then add a regression test asserting getPlatformAnalytics's loan_book for a seeded group equals the correlated-subquery value, because this class has already recurred after being fixed once and no test caught it.
verified.note: Fully reproduced on live data, exact figures. Strengthened by an in-repo comment proving the team already found, measured and fixed this identical bug (same 30x, same two numbers) in a sibling service, leaving admin.service.ts as the surviving instance.

verified.title: 98.4% of M-Pesa reconciliation runs find nothing yet each opens an audit row and two write transactions — 34,656 junk rows
verified.evidence:
Code re-read: lib/services/mpesa-reconciliation.service.ts:115-121 INSERTs a mpesa_reconciliations row with status='running' BEFORE any check for work; the stale-STK scan only happens afterwards at :128-142; the completion UPDATE fires unconditionally after the loop.

Live prod, re-run: `select reconciliation_type,status,count(*), count(*) filter (where coalesce(transactions_checked,0)=0 and coalesce(mismatches_found,0)=0 and coalesce(resolved_count,0)=0) from mpesa_reconciliations group by 1,2` -> stk/completed: 35,233 runs, of which 34,656 (98.36%) recorded 0 checked / 0 mismatches / 0 resolved.

pg_stat_statements corroboration, all re-measured — and the DB cost is LARGER than the finder quantified:
  INSERT INTO mpesa_reconciliations (...) VALUES ($1,$2,$3) RETURNING id — 35,236 calls, 206,310 ms (3.4 min)
  UPDATE mpesa_reconciliations SET status=$6, transactions_checked=$1, ... — 35,237 calls, 20,806 ms
  SELECT id, checkout_request_id FROM mpesa_stk_requests WHERE status=$2 AND initiated_at<$1 LIMIT $3 — 35,230 calls returning 577 rows TOTAL (0.0164 rows/call)
  Combined: 234,027 ms = 3.9 min = 1.1% of total DB exec time, plus ~70,473 of 629,293 BEGINs (11.2% of every transaction the database has served).

Scale control: the platform has 49 payments, 46 mpesa_stk_requests rows total, and ZERO currently pending. mpesa_reconciliations is 7,144 kB total relation size (the finder said 4.3 MB; that is the heap, not the indexes).
Schedule confirmed at lib/jobs/index.ts:133-135 with a five-minute dedup bucket, and lib/jobs/types.ts:14 comments it as "every 5 min".
verified.impact: ~70,500 write transactions and 35,230 scan statements over 121 days to discover nothing 98.4% of the time, permanently retaining 35,233 information-free rows in 7 MB. That is 11.2% of every transaction the database has processed and 1.1% of its execution time, against a platform that has processed 49 payments in total. It also burns a job-queue turn every five minutes in a queue Sentry KITABUYETU-1 reports as starving with 2,899 mpesa_reconcile jobs pending and the oldest 10 days old.
verified.recommendation: Invert the order in runReconciliation: run the stale-STK scan first, return early when it returns nothing, and only INSERT the mpesa_reconciliations row when there is actually work. That deletes ~98% of the writes with no behaviour change. Add a retention sweep for existing no-ops (`DELETE FROM mpesa_reconciliations WHERE transactions_checked=0 AND mismatches_found=0 AND resolved_count=0 AND created_at < now() - interval '7 days'`). Back the schedule off from every 5 minutes to every 30 — 577 stale STK rows in four months, and zero pending right now, does not justify 288 passes a day.
verified.note: Reproduced, and the database cost is materially higher than the finder reported (they gave no ms figure; the INSERT alone is 206 s). One citation corrected: the finder attributed the unconditional completion UPDATE to lines :323-331 — that range is inside sweepPaybillTransactions, which begins at :223. runReconciliation's own completion UPDATE is at :190-198. The substance is unaffected.

verified.title: 41 Promise.all blocks issue queries on a single PoolClient, which node-postgres serializes — the parallelism is cosmetic
verified.evidence:
The mechanism is real and I verified it against the installed driver, not from memory: node_modules/pg is version 8.20.0, and lib/client.js:579-599 `_pulseQueryQueue()` dispatches only when `this.readyForQuery === true`, sets it false while a query is in flight, and otherwise parks the query on `_queryQueue`. A PoolClient wraps one connection, so N concurrent client.query() calls on it execute strictly in sequence.

I re-scanned app/api and lib with my own matcher rather than trusting the count, and — importantly — separated blocks whose members run on ONE client from blocks whose members each open their own withAdminDb (which ARE genuinely parallel). Result: 41 same-client blocks (finder said 43), plus 3 genuinely-parallel ones (report-email.service.ts:94, delivery-tracking.service.ts:174, app/api/v1/email/logs/route.ts:40) that the finder correctly kept out of this finding.

The finder UNDERSTATED the worst case. Ranked by query count, the top same-client blocks are:
  lib/services/analytics.service.ts:141 — 15 queries (finder said 5), destructuring 15 results and closing at :341, under a comment at :122-124 that literally reads "Run every aggregation in parallel"
  lib/services/admin.service.ts:200 — 7; :379 — 6; sms-analytics.service.ts:65 — 6; analytics.service.ts:466 — 5; admin-organizations.service.ts:141, admin.service.ts:295/1108/1306, report-email... — 4 each
The credit-scores compound case is real as described: computeComponents at :368-389 wraps 8 component functions in Promise.all on one client, componentLoanRepayment at :448-451 adds its own inner Promise.all of 2, and recomputeAll's loop at :151 calls it once per member inside a single withTransaction opened at :140.

WHERE THE IMPACT CLAIM FAILS — two things I checked that the finder did not:
(1) Almost every headline offender is behind a Redis cache. admin.service.ts:199 `cached(..., 90)`, :294 `cached(..., 60)`, :378 `cached(..., 20)`, :1305 `cached(..., 120)`, analytics.service.ts:119 `cached(..., 60)`. So the serialized round trips are paid on a cache MISS, not "every one of these endpoints" on every request. sms-analytics.service.ts:65 is the notable uncached one.
(2) The credit-scores "worst compound case" has essentially never executed. credit_scores holds 14 rows, last computed 2026-08-12; `INSERT INTO credit_scores` shows 14 calls total across the 121-day window. The finder's "a 37-member group is ~370 strictly-sequential round trips" is hypothetical — 37 is the platform's TOTAL member count across 9 groups, and the largest single group has 9 members, so the real worst case ever run is ~90 round trips, once, three weeks ago.
(3) I cannot measure the Vercel-to-Supavisor RTT from this position, so the "sum instead of max" penalty has no measured magnitude. Server-side these queries are near-free (the tables hold 9 groups / 37 members).
verified.impact: Real but small today. On a cache miss the affected admin/analytics endpoints pay the sum of their query latencies instead of the max — worst case 15 sequential round trips on analytics.service.ts:141 — and that happens at most once per 20-120 seconds per endpoint, on a platform with 9 groups. There is no measurable database-side cost. The genuine harm is maintenance-shaped: the code reads as optimized (one block is even commented "Run every aggregation in parallel"), so nobody revisits it, and the penalty grows linearly with per-endpoint query count as the dashboards accrete panels.
verified.recommendation: Collapse each block into ONE statement using scalar subqueries or CTEs — `SELECT (SELECT ...) AS groups, (SELECT ...) AS members, ...`. That is a strict improvement, removes the round trips entirely, and is easiest exactly where the members are independent scalar aggregates (admin.service.ts:200/295/379). Start with analytics.service.ts:141 (15 queries) and sms-analytics.service.ts:65 (6 queries, uncached), which is where the real latency lives. Fix the misleading comment at analytics.service.ts:122-124 in the same change. Leave credit-scores alone for now — it has run 14 times in four months.
verified.note: OVERSTATED, not refuted. The mechanism, the driver evidence and the code sites all check out, and the worst block is three times bigger than reported (15 queries, not 5). The severity is inflated because the finder did not check for the `cached()` wrappers around the very endpoints it names, and its most alarming example (credit-score recompute over a 37-member group) describes a group size that does not exist on this platform and a code path that has run 14 times in 121 days. Downgraded medium -> low.

verified.title: Every templated email makes 4 separate uncached transactions, two of which query permanently-empty tables ~24,500 times each for 0 rows
verified.evidence:
Code path re-traced end to end: lib/services/email.service.ts:22 sendTemplatedEmail -> renderTemplate (lib/email/templates/engine.ts:134) which calls loadBranding at :141 and loadDbTemplate at :142, each opening its OWN withAdminDb (engine.ts:30-41 and :67-75) -> then lib/email/adapters/resend.ts:19-37 INSERTs the queued log in a third transaction -> then :65-70 or :78-83 UPDATEs it in a fourth. Four connection acquisitions, four BEGIN/COMMIT pairs, per send.

pg_stat_statements, re-measured over the 121-day window:
  `SELECT subject, body FROM email_templates WHERE template_key=$1 ...` — 24,544 calls, rows returned: 0
  `SELECT sender_name, logo_url, primary_color, footer_text FROM group_email_branding WHERE group_id=$1` — 24,362 calls, rows returned: 0
  `SELECT * FROM email_schedules WHERE is_active=$1 AND next_run_at <= NOW() ...` (scheduler.service.ts:9) — 25,721 calls, rows returned: 0
  Total 74,627 statements, every one a full connect/BEGIN/COMMIT cycle, all returning nothing.
Falsification control (the finder's, which I re-ran): the `rows` column is genuinely populated for other entries in this same view — 210,957 for the retry SELECT, 48,260 for the email_logs INSERT — so 0 is a real zero and not an unpopulated column.
Data control: `select count(*) from email_templates` = 0, `group_email_branding` = 0, `email_schedules` = 0. All three tables are empty and have always been.
Stranded-row claim re-measured: 4,007 email_logs rows sit permanently at status='queued' (3,677 group_verification_link + 268 weekly_summary + 37 staff_operational_alert + 25 account_statement), so the pre-insert-then-update design is not delivering the crash-safety it was written for.
lib/redis/index.ts:196 exports `cached<T>()` and admin.service.ts already uses it, so the fix has no new dependency.
verified.impact: 74,627 statements — each its own connection acquisition, BEGIN and COMMIT — asking three permanently-empty tables the same question, indefinitely. Because two of these are 2 of the 4 transactions per templated send, caching them roughly halves the email path's connection-acquisition rate. Sizing caveat I verified: only ~24,500 of the 48,260 email_logs INSERTs go through renderTemplate (the React-rendered statement/report paths bypass it), so this is 'every templated send', not literally every send. Note also that the overwhelming majority of that 24,500 is generated by the retry loop in finding #1 — fix that first and this volume drops by roughly an order of magnitude on its own.
verified.recommendation: Wrap loadDbTemplate and loadBranding in the existing `cached()` helper with a 5-minute TTL keyed on (templateKey, groupId, locale) and groupId, invalidated on template/branding writes. Cache the negative result too — DEFAULT_TEMPLATES already supplies the fallback, so an empty table is a perfectly cacheable answer. Guard processDueSchedules with a cheap EXISTS probe, or stop scheduling it while email_schedules is empty. Merge resend.ts's queued-INSERT and status-UPDATE into a single post-send INSERT; the pre-insert exists to survive a crash mid-send but has left 4,007 rows stranded at 'queued', so it is not achieving that today.
verified.note: Reproduced exactly, including the falsification control on the pg_stat_statements `rows` column. Two clarifications added: the '4 transactions per email' applies to the templated path (~24.5k of 48.3k sends), and most of the volume is downstream of finding #1, so this should be sequenced after it rather than treated as an independent win.

verified.title: Near-zero connection reuse: 529,613 pooler authentications against 629,293 transactions (0.84 new connections per transaction)
verified.evidence:
The ratio is real and I re-measured it: `SELECT * FROM pgbouncer.get_auth($1)` = 529,613 calls / 289,978 ms; `begin` = 629,293; `commit` = 610,475. That is 0.842 pooler authentications per transaction, matching the finder's 0.845.

Mechanism confirmed in code: lib/db/index.ts:64-74 builds the pool with `idleTimeoutMillis: 10_000` and `max: env.DB_POOL_MAX`, whose default is 3 (lib/env.ts:21 — the finder cited :22). withAdminDb (:172-187) and withDb (:137-154) each take a fresh `pool.connect()` per call, and the codebase calls them per-statement in the email and reconciliation paths.

WHERE THE MAGNITUDE FAILS. The finder's closing claim is that "every finding above that says 'one transaction per row' is also a finding about this number", and its recommendation is to "attack the call-site multiplier" identified in the write-loop finding. I measured those call sites and they contribute essentially nothing:
  email_preferences table: 0 rows — the PUT loop has never written a row
  bill_manager_invoices: 0 rows — that loop has never run
  email_campaign_recipients: 0 rows — campaign.service.ts:104's loop has never inserted
  `INSERT INTO accounts`: 16 calls in 121 days
Combined, the four "per-row transaction" sites account for ~16 of 629,293 BEGINs (0.003%). The churn is driven almost entirely by two things: the email retry loop (~194k transactions, 31%) and the no-op reconciliation (~70k, 11%). Also, get_auth's 289,978 ms is only 1.39% of total database exec time, not a headline cost.
verified.impact: 529,613 TCP + TLS + SCRAM handshakes from Lambda over 121 days, of which roughly 42% are attributable to two runaway background jobs. The measurable database cost is 290 seconds (1.4% of exec time); the client-side handshake cost is billed as Vercel function wall-clock and is not observable from here, so the finder's 'order of hours' is an estimate, not a measurement. The right way to read this number is as a symptom metric for findings #1 and #4, not as an independent problem with its own fix.
verified.recommendation: Do not start here. Fix findings #1 and #4 and re-measure — those two alone should take get_auth from ~530k toward ~330k. Raising `idleTimeoutMillis` from 10s to 60s in lib/db/index.ts:67 is a cheap, safe complement (Supavisor absorbs the concurrency and DB_POOL_MAX is only 3), and the get_auth-to-begin ratio is a good standing health metric — it should fall well below 0.5 once the two loops are bounded. Ignore the per-row write loops as a churn lever; they measurably are not one.
verified.note: OVERSTATED. The ratio, the mechanism and the code are all correct and reproduced, but the finding presents connection churn as an independent problem with its own call-site fix list, and I disproved the fix list: the four write-loop sites it points at have produced ~16 transactions in 121 days against 629,293 total. This is a derived metric of findings #1 and #4, and its own DB cost is 1.4%. Downgraded medium -> low.

verified.title: Bulk member import runs 3-4 sequential queries per CSV row inside one transaction, with a bcrypt hash per new member
verified.evidence:
Code fully confirmed. lib/services/import.service.ts:274 commitMembers wraps everything in a single withTransaction at :278. The per-row loop starts at :297 and issues: a duplicate-in-group check at :301 (group_members JOIN members on phone), an existing-member lookup at :317, then either an UPDATE at :325 or an INSERT at :346, then linkMemberToGroup at :367 which adds one more query. So 3-5 sequential round trips per row, all inside one open transaction. MAX_ROWS is defined at :21 with a 5,000 default. On the request path via app/api/v1/import/[jobId]/commit/route.ts:24. The file's own preview path already solved the analogous problem — :131 reads "Counties cached once per import to avoid N queries" — and the commit path never got it.

EVIDENCE THE FINDER MISSED that makes the code concern worse: line 345 calls `await bcrypt.hash(generateTempPassword(), BCRYPT_RND)` (default 10 rounds, :22) for every NEW member, inside the same transaction. At ~60-100 ms per hash that is 5-8 minutes of pure CPU for 5,000 new members, independent of round trips — a bigger term than the database work the finding is about.

EVIDENCE THAT DEFLATES THE IMPACT: I checked what has actually run. `select count(*) from import_jobs` = 7, and `max(jsonb_array_length(preview_rows))` across all of them = 6. The largest import ever attempted on this platform is six rows. Total platform membership is 36-37 members across 9 groups. There is no production incident here, and none is imminent.
verified.impact: Latent. Today the worst real import is 6 rows and costs ~30 round trips. The forward-looking concern is sound and worth writing down: a 5,000-row import would issue 15,000-25,000 strictly sequential round trips plus 5,000 bcrypt hashes inside ONE transaction, which cannot finish in a Vercel function budget — and because it is one transaction, a timeout rolls back every row already imported, so a large import can neither succeed nor partially succeed. That matters the first time a customer onboards with a real member roster, which is exactly the moment you least want to discover it.
verified.recommendation: Hoist the duplicate and existing-member checks out of the loop: one query fetching all (phone -> member_id) pairs for the group into a Map replaces :301 and :317. Batch the inserts at :346 into multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES (...),(...) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING id` in chunks of 500. Move the bcrypt hashing out of the transaction entirely (compute all hashes first, or drop the temp password in favour of a reset token). Then move commit off the request path into the job queue for anything above a few hundred rows. None of this is urgent — schedule it before the first real customer onboarding, not this week.
verified.note: OVERSTATED on severity, not on facts. Every cited line is accurate and I found an additional cost (per-row bcrypt inside the transaction) that reinforces the code argument. But 'medium' overstates a path whose largest execution in the platform's history is a 6-row import, on a platform with 36 members. Downgraded medium -> low and reframed as pre-onboarding work rather than a live defect.

verified.title: Cron fan-out services walk groups and members one at a time with a network send per item, no batching and no resumability
verified.evidence:
Structure confirmed at every cited site. lib/services/report-email.service.ts:84-158 sendWeeklySummaries: one query for active groups at :85, then PER GROUP four separate withAdminDb transactions in a Promise.all at :94-130 plus an officers lookup at :140, then a sequential per-officer send at :149. I checked this specific Promise.all's members and — unlike the blocks in finding #5 — each one really does open its own withAdminDb, so the finder is right that it requests 4 concurrent pool connections against DB_POOL_MAX=3 and the fourth queues.
lib/services/statement-email.service.ts:112-140 sendAllGroupMemberStatements: sequential per-group loop at :121 wrapping sendMemberStatements, whose per-member loop at :83 makes a provider call at the leaf with no concurrency, no cursor and no cap. (Fair to the code: the snapshot and transaction data ARE pre-batched into Maps before that loop, so it is a send fan-out, not a query N+1.)
Same shape at governance.service.ts:405-415 and mpesa-reports.service.ts:26-40 / :99.
pg_stat_statements corroborates the per-group multiplication exactly as claimed: `SELECT COALESCE(SUM(principal_amount),$2) ... FROM loans WHERE group_id=$1` = 165 calls and `SELECT COUNT(*) AS total FROM group_members WHERE group_id=$1 AND joined_at >= ...` = 165 calls, i.e. once per group per run where one GROUP BY would have run once. `SELECT id, name FROM groups WHERE is_active = $1` = 851 calls.

WHERE THE IMPACT CLAIM FAILS. The finder attributes concrete production damage to this shape: "That is why account_statement shows 64 failed / 24 stranded-queued rows and weekly_summary 2,110 failed rows for 4 distinct recipients." I checked the counts (69 failed / 25 queued, and 2,110 / 268 — close enough) and then checked the CAUSE, which the finder did not. Every one of those failures carries a Resend error string: "You have reached your daily email sending quota", "Greeting never received", or "The ezzahcomm.co.ke domain is not verified". None of them is a duplicate re-send from a job re-run. The weekly_summary rows in particular are being generated by the retry loop in finding #1 — email_weekly_summary last COMPLETED on 2026-08-24, yet weekly_summary rows are created daily through 2026-09-04. The causal chain is refuted.
Current-state control: email_weekly_summary shows 13 completed against 1 failed, so the job does finish today.
verified.impact: Structurally real, currently harmless. Each job costs O(groups x members) sequential network calls with no checkpoint and no per-recipient idempotency key, so a timeout mid-run re-sends everything from the start when resetStuckJobs (lib/jobs/db.ts:136) releases it. At 9 groups and 37 members that is a handful of calls and the job completes; the cost grows linearly with customers and will exceed a function budget well before the platform is large. The DB-side waste is 330 avoidable statements over 121 days.
verified.recommendation: Replace the per-group aggregates with a single `GROUP BY group_id` query returning every group's numbers in one round trip (drops report-email from 5 transactions per group to 2 for the whole run). For the fan-out, enqueue one job per group rather than one job for the whole platform, so a timeout loses one group's work instead of all of it and the queue's own retry/backoff applies at the right granularity. Add a per-recipient idempotency key so a re-run cannot re-send. Low priority relative to findings #1, #3 and #4.
verified.note: OVERSTATED. The code shape, the line references and the 165-call corroboration are all accurate and reproduced — including the DB_POOL_MAX=3 detail, which the finder got right where a naive scan would have gotten it wrong. But the impact paragraph's load-bearing evidence is refuted: the account_statement and weekly_summary failure counts it cites as proof of re-run duplication are Resend quota/domain errors, and the weekly_summary rows are produced by finding #1's retry loop rather than by this job at all. With that removed, the finding is a forward-looking scalability observation on a job that completes today. Downgraded medium -> low.

verified.title: sweepPaybillTransactions has no scheduler at all — it has executed exactly once in the platform's lifetime
verified.evidence:
I re-ran the reachability analysis rather than trusting it. `grep -rn 'runReconciliation|sweepPaybillTransactions' app lib` returns: sweepPaybillTransactions is defined at lib/services/mpesa-reconciliation.service.ts:223, re-exported through lib/services/mpesa.service.ts:90, and called from exactly two places — app/api/v1/mpesa/reconcile/route.ts:41 and :55, both inside a manual, authenticated HTTP endpoint. lib/jobs/handlers.ts:246-251 wires the scheduled `mpesa_reconcile` job to runReconciliation only. Positive control on the absence: `grep -rn 'paybill_sweep|mpesa_paybill'` across lib/jobs returns nothing, while the same grep for 'mpesa_reconcile' returns 8 hits across handlers.ts, index.ts and types.ts — so the matcher works and the gap is real. lib/jobs/types.ts contains no paybill sweep job type.

Live prod, re-run: `select reconciliation_type,count(*),min(created_at),max(created_at) from mpesa_reconciliations group by 1` -> paybill_sweep: 1 row, 2026-07-29 18:23:57.712558+00, which is simultaneously the oldest and the newest. Against stk: 35,233 runs, newest 2026-09-05 07:35. balance_drift: 386 runs, newest today.
Context: mpesa_unrouted currently holds 12 rows.
The function's own doc comment at :218-222 establishes it is fully idempotent ("mpesa_unrouted.receipt is UNIQUE, so a receipt is queued at most once regardless of how often the sweep runs"), so scheduling it carries no correctness risk.
verified.impact: Inverted priority in the reconciliation subsystem. The sweep that finds nothing 98.4% of the time runs every five minutes and has burned 70,000 transactions doing it; the sweep that actually detects completed inbound C2B paybill transactions with no domain record — the precise failure class behind the platform's known unrouted-payment work — has never been scheduled and has run once, five and a half weeks ago, manually. This is distinct from the job-queue starvation in Sentry KITABUYETU-1: there is no queue entry to starve, so no amount of throughput work will ever make it run. Detection of lost paybill money is currently manual-only and nobody is doing it manually.
verified.recommendation: Add a `mpesa_paybill_sweep` job type in lib/jobs/types.ts, wire it in handlers.ts to sweepPaybillTransactions, and enqueue it hourly in lib/jobs/index.ts alongside the existing mpesa_reconcile block at :133. Idempotency is already guaranteed by the UNIQUE receipt constraint, so this needs no new safety work. In the same change, demote runReconciliation from every-5-minutes to every-30 — 577 stale STK rows in four months, and zero pending right now, does not justify 288 passes a day.
verified.note: Fully reproduced, including a positive control proving the absence of the job wiring is real rather than a failed grep. Strictly this is a coverage/correctness gap rather than an optimization one, but it is the natural companion fix to finding #4 and should ship in the same change.

verified.title: Write loops that open one full transaction per row instead of one multi-row statement
verified.evidence:
All four code sites confirmed by reading them:
- app/api/v1/email/preferences/route.ts:46 — `for (const pref of prefs)` with a withAdminDb at :47, plus a `.catch()` at :60 that opens a SECOND transaction with a different UPDATE on conflict (worst case 2N).
- lib/services/campaign.service.ts:103-113 — one withAdminDb transaction per campaign recipient, uncapped by group size.
- app/api/v1/mpesa/bill-manager/route.ts:155-156 — up to 100 sequential INSERTs, correctly noted by the finder as sharing one OUTER withAdminDb, so N round trips rather than N transactions.
- lib/services/accounting.service.ts:238-246 seedDefaultAccountsInTx — sequential INSERTs over DEFAULT_ACCOUNTS, which I counted programmatically at exactly 20 entries (declared at :15).

WHAT I MEASURED THAT THE FINDING DID NOT. These loops have barely executed:
  email_preferences: 0 rows in production. The PUT loop has never successfully written anything — which also means the ON CONFLICT target problem masked by the :60 fallback is untested in production.
  email_campaign_recipients: 0 rows. campaign.service.ts:104 has never inserted.
  bill_manager_invoices: 0 rows. That loop has never run.
  accounts: 165 rows exist, but `INSERT INTO accounts (group_id, account_code, ...)` shows only 16 calls in the entire 121-day window — the rest predate it.
So all four sites together account for roughly 16 transactions out of 629,293 BEGINs.
verified.impact: Negligible today by measurement, not by estimate: ~16 transactions in 121 days across all four sites. The finder's claim that "these are the multipliers behind the connection-churn ratio" is wrong by five orders of magnitude — the churn comes from the email retry loop and the no-op reconciliation. What does deserve attention is smaller and different: email_preferences has zero rows, so a member has apparently never successfully saved preferences, and the try/catch-into-a-second-transaction at :60 is masking rather than handling whatever ON CONFLICT problem causes that.
verified.recommendation: Deprioritise as a performance item. Do investigate app/api/v1/email/preferences/route.ts separately as a possible correctness bug: zero rows in email_preferences with a fallback path that quietly swaps INSERT ... ON CONFLICT for a bare UPDATE is the signature of a broken conflict target, not of a slow loop. When any of these paths is next touched, collapse it into a single multi-row `INSERT ... VALUES (...),(...) ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`, which for preferences also removes the second-transaction fallback entirely.
verified.note: OVERSTATED. Every code site is real and accurately cited (DEFAULT_ACCOUNTS is exactly 20), and the finder was honest in calling it low severity. But the impact rationale — that these loops are what drives the connection-churn number — is refuted by measurement: three of the four target tables have zero rows and the fourth shows 16 inserts in 121 days. The genuinely interesting signal here is a possible correctness bug in email/preferences, which the performance framing obscured.

verified.title: Tenant reads cost 6 round trips for 1 statement because setTenantLocals issues three separate set_config calls
verified.evidence:
The code the finding describes exists, but the code path it costs is unreachable.

What is true: lib/db/index.ts:121-131 setTenantLocals does run `SELECT set_config($1,$2,TRUE)` three times sequentially (four when organizationId is present, :128-130). pg_stat_statements shows `SELECT set_config($1, $2, $3)` = 6,591 calls and `SELECT set_config($1,$2,$3)` = 6,409 calls, 13,000 total — matching the finder's figure exactly, and implying ~4,333 tenant transactions in 121 days (~36/day).

What is NOT true is the finding's central claim. It rests on lib/db/index.ts:192-202's `query(ctx, sql, params)` helper, which wraps ONE caller statement in withDb and therefore costs BEGIN + 3 set_config + the statement + COMMIT = 6 round trips for 1 statement. I searched for its callers with a parser that handles multi-line named imports across lib/, app/, components/ and scripts/: **zero files import `query` from '@/lib/db'.** It has no production callers at all.
Positive control, because a check that cannot fail is worthless: the same scanner, over the same files, reports withAdminDb imported in 109 files, withDb in 46, withTransaction in 32, `type TenantContext` in 41 and `pool` in 8. It finds named imports correctly, so the zero is a real zero. (A few files under __tests__/ do import from '@/lib/db'; nothing on a request path does.)

What survives: real tenant traffic goes through withDb/withTransaction (234 call sites), where a transaction containing N statements costs N + 5 round trips, not 6-per-1. Collapsing the three set_config calls saves 2 round trips per TRANSACTION, not per statement. The measured server-side cost of all 13,000 set_config calls is 800 ms combined (346 ms + 454 ms) across 121 days. The finding's impact figure — "20-60 ms of pure latency added to every request in the product, user-visible" — is an unmeasured assumption: I have no way to observe Vercel-to-Supavisor RTT from this position, and at ~36 tenant transactions per day "every request in the product" does not describe this platform's traffic either.
verified.impact: None as stated. The 6-round-trips-for-1-statement path has no callers. The residual real effect is 2 avoidable round trips per tenant transaction, on ~36 transactions a day, costing 800 ms of server-side time in four months.
verified.recommendation: Do not schedule this as written. If the three set_config calls are ever collapsed as a drive-by, `SELECT set_config($1,$2,TRUE), set_config($3,$4,TRUE), set_config($5,$6,TRUE)` is correct, still parameterised, still transaction-local, and safe inside the existing BEGIN — it saves 2 round trips per transaction, not per statement. Separately, consider deleting the unused `query()` export at lib/db/index.ts:192-202 so it stops attracting analysis; if it is kept for tests, say so in a comment.
verified.note: REFUTED. The set_config mechanism and the 13,000-call volume are both real and I reproduced them, but the finding's headline, its title, its magnitude and its recommendation all depend on the single-statement `query()` helper, which has zero importers anywhere outside tests — the code path is unreachable. Corrected to the real shape (2 round trips per transaction, 234 call sites, ~36 transactions/day, 800 ms total), the finding is too small to act on, and the '20-60 ms on every request' impact figure was never measured.

verified.title: The subscription gate's allow-list-only cache means an unentitled group re-queries the database on every request
verified.evidence:
Code confirmed line-for-line. lib/auth/subscription-gate.ts:233-234 reads `const products = await loadActiveProducts(auth.groupId); if (products.size > 0) remember(auth.groupId, products);` — a group resolving to an empty set is never cached, so every one of its requests runs loadActiveProducts (:177-186), a full withAdminDb transaction. assertSubscriptionActive is defined at :217 and is called from lib/auth/middleware.ts:67, which the surrounding comment confirms is the single chokepoint every tenant route passes through (withRole, withOneOf, withPermission and withAnyPermission all delegate to it).
The same applies to a second deny case the finder did not mention: a group that IS entitled but not for THIS route's product also fails `satisfies(cached.products)` at :229 and re-reads.

Live prod, re-run: `select g.name, g.is_active, coalesce(string_agg(distinct s.product||':'||s.status,', '),'(none)') from groups g left join subscriptions s on s.group_id=g.id group by 1,2` -> `coinbankcrypto` has NO subscription rows at all; `PROD VERIFY - safe to delete` and `VERIFY 098-100 - safe to deactivate` hold only kitabu_yetu:expired. The remaining 6 of 9 groups hold an active subscription and are served from the in-process Map.
One factual correction: the finder wrote "two of those are deactivated". They are not — all 9 groups have is_active = true. Only their NAMES say they are safe to deactivate.
The trade-off is deliberate and documented: the doc comment at :186-212 explains that caching a product set naively would 402 a group that just paid for a second product ("I paid and it's still broken, one product later") and explicitly accepts the re-query cost on the deny path.
verified.impact: Bounded and small today: 3 of 9 groups, and requests from those groups terminate in a 402 rather than proceeding, so a client showing a paywall does not loop. This is a shape-of-failure finding rather than a live cost. It matters because it is the mode that grows badly: the moment a cohort of subscriptions lapses — which has happened on this platform before, with all 5 production groups expiring at once — every request from every lapsed group becomes an uncached database transaction on the single hottest code path in the application.
verified.recommendation: Add a short NEGATIVE cache — 5-10 seconds, deliberately far below the 60s positive TTL — covering both deny cases (empty set, and entitled-but-wrong-product). That preserves the load-bearing correctness rule the file documents at :186-212 while capping the worst case at ~6-12 queries per minute per lapsed group instead of one per request. Do not cache the empty set at the full CACHE_TTL_MS; the doc comment explains precisely why that reintroduces the bug it was written to prevent.
verified.note: Confirmed on both code and live data, at the low severity the finder assigned. One data claim corrected (no group is deactivated; all 9 have is_active = true) and one case added that the finder missed (entitled-but-wrong-product also bypasses the cache). Worth noting in the finder's favour: it read the file's doc comment and proposed a fix that respects the documented correctness constraint rather than one that would re-break it.
